title: Recsys Keynote: Improving Recommendation Systems & Search in the Age of LLMs - Eugene Yan, Amazon
talk_summary: A recsys keynote covering semantic IDs, LM-generated synthetic data/labels, and unified multi-task models, drawn from papers at Quaishou, Indeed, Spotify, Netflix, and Etsy. The transferable core is a cost/latency cascade: use a strong expensive model to label, then distill into a cheap fast classifier for production.

takeaways.what_they_do: Indeed used GPT-4 to label good/bad job recommendations at ~90% precision/recall, then fine-tuned a cheaper model on those labels, then distilled a lightweight classifier for real-time filtering.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they distilled a lightweight classifier on the fine tetune GBD 2.5 labels and this lightweight classifier was able to achieve very high performance
takeaways.numbers: GPT-4 ~90% P/R at 32s; fine-tuned 3.5 at 1/4 cost, 6.7s; distilled classifier 0.86 AUROC, <200ms; bad recs cut 20%, applications +4%, unsubscribes -5%

takeaways.what_they_do: Indeed tracked precision of the 'bad' filter because low precision meant throwing out good recommendations; they optimized the filter against that specific business cost, not raw accuracy.
takeaways.evidence_quote: only 63% of them were actually bad ... they were throwing out 37% of recommendations
takeaways.numbers: GPT-3.5 precision 0.63 → 37% good items wrongly rejected

takeaways.what_they_do: They tried open models first (poor), then strong model (good but slow/costly), then progressively cheaper models, measuring quality at each tier before committing.

takeaways.technique: LM augments conventional pipeline, not replaces it
takeaways.what_they_do: Spotify generated candidate queries with conventional extraction/mining, using the LM only to generate natural-language variants where needed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Take whatever you have with conventional techniques that work really well and use the LM to augment it when you need it. Don't use the LM for everything at the start.

takeaways.what_they_do: Netflix's unified ranker used one input schema (user, item, query, country, task) with imputation for missing fields, letting one model serve multiple tasks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you are able to find a data schema where all your use cases and all your features can use the same input
